ov: Four species of spiny, egg-laying mammals from Australia and New Guinea, also called spiny anteaters. Their snouts carry electrosensors for finding buried prey, and they have long sticky tongues but no teeth. Their young are called puggles.

why.et: The rare long-beaked echidnas of New Guinea are hunted for food.

wt: Females about 4.5 kg, males about 6 kg
rg: Australia, including Tasmania, and New Guinea.
df: Short-beaked echidnas eat mostly ants and termites; long-beaked echidnas eat worms and insect larvae.

cf.tip: Both are spiny, but the echidna lays eggs and is not closely related to hedgehogs.

fx: A captive echidna lived to 50, very long for a mammal its size.
The mother lays a single leathery egg straight into her pouch.

_cf.tip: Both are spiny, but the echidna lays eggs and is not closely related to hedgehogs.
The only other egg-laying mammals are the four species of echidna, which are covered in spines and live on land.
